title: Google My Business API: Access, Limits & Setup (2026)
summary: Google My Business API is free but requires approval before requests work. Understand the approval process, quota limits, and request procedures.
body_markdown:
## Automate recurring Business Profile tasks with Activepieces


Once failures are rare, what remains is repetition. Activepieces, a workflow automation tool, can run that repetition for you: scheduled review pulls, new-review alerts and scheduled posts, with no code to maintain.


A run costs 1 credit however many steps it has, and the free plan includes 1,000 credits a month. Google still controls approval and quota.


Though the API is now documented under Business Profile, code and forum threads still use the older name. Activepieces doesn't change what sits underneath.


Its steps call the same Google API with the same OAuth credentials you already set up, and the MIT-licensed core is on GitHub, with 25,683 stars, if you want to read how a step is built.


If your project hasn't been approved, the workflow fails the way a script would, with the same permission error. Do the access steps first, then build the flow.


Three calls matter for automation: listing reviews, replying to them, and creating local posts.


Activepieces has 750 integrations, roughly 60% of them community-contributed, and the figure is counted directly from the` packages/pieces/community` directory of its MIT-licensed open source monorepo on GitHub, not published as a marketing number, so you can see that most of the platform's reach comes from volunteer effort.


A Google Business Profile integration either has a folder in that directory or it doesn't, and where one covers the call you need, use it. Where it doesn't, an HTTP step sends the request directly, using your credentials.


Start with the review list. A flow that reads reviews on a schedule is the easiest to verify, and it proves your approval works before anything is published.


Google doesn't charge per call. The limit you hit is quota, and a workflow tool doesn't raise it.


A missed quota error costs more than a slow flow does. An angry one-star review that sits unseen all weekend because a run failed quietly is a bad ticket, so route failed runs to an alert as well.


Here's how the work divides: a scheduled review pull, a new-review alert to Slack or email and a scheduled local post suit Activepieces, where unlimited flows on every plan, free included, let each one be its own flow, while high-volume multi-location sync still needs code.


The first three are a handful of calls on a timer, where one failed run is easy to see and retry. Sync across many locations needs batching, backoff and careful quota use, and those are easier to control in code you own.


That points to the practical order.


Build the review pull and the alert in Activepieces, which costs $0 on the free plan with no card needed, watch what quota and permission errors actually appear, and move to code only when volume demands it, so you discover any limitations at zero cost before engineering effort.
